comments.name: Dennis Delaney
comments.body: I laughed out loud when I saw the SNL sketch. Hilarious. I am not a sister rather an oldest brother. For the past 9 years I have been the full time caregiver for my elderly now late mother. I moved from NYC to Southern Arizona to make sure that my mother did not have to spend one second in a nursing home. It has been the most emotionally, mentally, physically, financially, and spiritually difficult thing that I have ever faced. A brutal experience. Now, 73 years old, who am I? Where do I go? How am I able? How do I start again? Planning to return to NYC which seems like a foreign country. The SNL sketch was brilliantly funny because it hit home for millions of Americans. I'm not a sister, but I am. Forward march...

Well I’m in this hell right now but balancing with three other sisters. I have no idea how a solo child does it. 

This is dark, but I think openness to MAID will grow significantly over the next 25 years because we’re simply not going to put our own families through this. And there will be much more aggressively protective advanced directives - ruling out many medical services given without a thought these days. Enough of celebrating longevity. 

I have a birth date and I have a death date at 78.

comments.name: Chris
comments.body: Australia doesn't just provide paid leave. They have a carer's payment or a carer's pension- depending on the assets of the carer. They actively provide services at home- help with bathing, cleaning, home maintenance, transport. The cost is heavily subsidized. It is done because its cheaper to keep older adults in their own homes. That is why both Australia and the US are spending about the same percentage of GDP- but Australians get much better value for their money.

comments.name: MS

comments.name: Barbara
comments.body:
I quit my job to take care of my father 30-years ago after he collapsed and was hospitalized for complications from congestive heart failure. My brother's only interest in my father was his inheritance and he was completely out of the picture while my mother had died 15-years earlier so my father was alone. I loved my father very much and promised him that he would never go to a nursing home. 

I don't regret my choice because I loved my father deeply and he was a wonderful man with a positive attitude and a great sense of humor. Our relationship deepened during this time and the memories of our conversations are still with me.

However, it was very hard for me to get back into the work force after his death and I lost years of salary, IRA investments, and social security payments. It's the latter that our government could do something about, but chooses not to and never will. There is no recognition that this service is labor, just as there is no recognition for the labor of stay-at-home mothers.

comments.name: Susan
comments.body: I was Sister-in-Law.  My husband was diagnosed with Parkinson's at 57 and died from its complications when he was 71.  As his wife I willingly took on caregiving responsibilities.  It was very difficult.  It broke my heart.  I was left exhausted, grief-stricken, almost destroyed byt the time he died.  I didn't expect help from his one remaining brother, who lived far away and was still employed.  But the brother, who loved my husband very much, constantly made excuses for not visiting.  I told him to please come before it was too late for my husband to communicate with him.  Well, he arrived too late.  His brother was 3 weeks away from death, though I didn't know that.  He was delirious.  He was in a nursing home for 3 days but was so miserable and the care was so poor that I brought him home.  When Brother arrived he panicked--"You can't take care of him!"  But I did take care of him, not very well sometimes, but I hung in there.  So I had to handle Brother's emotions while my husband made his final trip to the hospital. Brother left, Husband died, and I somehow did all that you have to do when your loved one dies.  Brother was too emotionally fragile to come to the memorial upon which I expended the last of my energy.  I wanted to honor the extraordinary man my husband had been. I know that Brother was truly traumatized and I felt for him.  But Wife's trauma was just part of her duty, not to be taken into any kind of consideration.

Term limits would be an excellent idea.  Australia's High Court judges retire at age 70.  "The immediate catalyst was the remarkable longevity of Justice Edward McTiernan. Appointed in 1930, McTiernan served for 46 years, longer than any judge of a final appellate court in the common-law world".

The supreme question for humanity is not whether AI can and/or will go rogue and destroy human civilization but whether we humans are secure enough in what we can agree are the essential elements of our humanity. I would place direct human experience and its concomitant personal knowledge at the top of any list of human necessities. We have yet to learn, despite developing and unleashing an array of technologies, notably nuclear weapons and those that despoil our environment, that just because we humans who prize free will can do something does not answer the moral quandary of whether we should do it. 

Put in classical philosophical terms: "An ought can neither be derived from an is, nor should it be without prior moral reflection."

comments.name: Emmanations
comments.body:
“Is it technically possible to verify whether an A.I. model is aligned enough to release?”

The progress on understanding what LLMs are doing is quickly improving. The area is called mechanistic interpretability. The past few months have improved by orders of magnitude. 

As I commented elsewhere here, the “thinking” tokens are how we can tell if a model is scheming, but the AI labs will not let us see those to prevent Chinese companies from using it to train their models. We need assurance that they have scheming detection in place. 

(The thinking tokens are how models organize their plan and choose options when making an answer.)

comments.name: David Sciascia

I'm 74 years old. My son recommended I use 1Password about 8 years ago to manage all my passwords and never looked back. Never had a usability issue, never been hacked. Unbelievably I have over 100 log-ins and they all use completely unique and the maximum number of password characters allowed, sone of them 50 characters long and all completely unguessable. I fairly regularly change my most important financial passwords. It takes about a minute and they all look somethng like this: VoqByzeBYTyXbiXfHNJYFfYawxcfYgabdErVCyQQDBbUrFbXHu

People who use variations of a few remembered passwords are just kidding themselves that they are secure.

comments.name: Angstrom Unit
comments.body: Here, a human gives good advice, but notice how defensive it is, as if we are under siege, which I guess we are.  A culture that lets a machine do its thinking, however, is intellectually bankrupt. We have reached that point and money is in the driver's seat, another artificial contrivance.  This is what happens when people reflexively accept the same set of preposterous beliefs: that the unhindered acquisition of enormous fortunes by a few is acceptable, even commendable, and not a clear and present threat; that they can produce whatever they want no matter what damage is done; that there’s nothing objectionable about a few billionaires owning the media and setting the political agenda; and that anyone who disputes such notions has no place in civil society. The direct results are massive deficits, the abandonment of public services and the dissolution of the commonwealth. In the US, we have Trump and the GOP's attempt to murder the truth, purge the public service, attack whole swathes of the population, mainly women, and terrorise millions of innocent people because of their immigration status (there is irony in the fact that this plan is positively Soviet in its scope and virulence). Back in the 1930’s J.M. Keynes predicted that, when the financial benefits of new technologies accrue only to the few, both the few and the losers will suffer a form of cognitive breakdown. It's happening. Surely there is a better way to manage our affairs.

I just received a notification from a vendor (the third company this year alone) informing me that THEIR data has been hacked and my info has been compromised.  Clearly, it doesn't matter how securely I maintain my own accounts, when everyone from my doctor's office, to state agencies, to my utility company are hacked and my personal info is stolen. For example, my cell phone provider was hacked four years ago and ALL of my personal information was stolen and made available on the dark web--from SS number to credit card number (all required by the cell phone provider in order to my establish my account). The cell phone company's apology to me? A $50 credit to my account.

comments.body:
There is a very important element I have yet to see deeply reported: WHY is Google pushing so hard to have AI in our schools? WHY is Google pushing so hard to learn how children learn? 

Every placed article I have seen written by Google’s newsroom highlights that Google AI scrapes data from the kids as much as it “gives back” in “educational” “outcomes.”

So WHY is Google pushing so hard on this? Because clearly they are getting something in return. And that is data from our children, who can’t even consent to their work being hoovered up to train computers to steal their future. THIS is the part that sickens me. 

Adults who use free software probably have some idea that their creative output isn’t owned by them in total. But kids? They don’t know that. And these monstrous bad actors masquerading as beneficent institutions shouldn’t be allowed to have free access to this “IP.” 

Parents at the very least should have a say as to what can and cannot be used out our childrens’ education journey, much as we are given a say about whether our child’s likeness can be used on a school website or social media platform. It’s beyond blackmail or extortion and it should be illegal.

comments.body: Baby boomer here.  The solution is simple but now impossible; Eliminate travel sports for youth, and go back to the youth sports model from the 50's thru 80's.  In those days, there were no "travel" sports,  The city recreational departments ran local team programs for football, baseball, and basketball, and teams competed locally in the city or town only.  There were age group programs parallel to junior high and high school teams.  If a kid wanted to play, there was a team somewhere he/she could make.  Team sports teach children lessons they can only learn on the field of competition, teamwork, belonging, spirit, physical and metal toughness, and compassion when your teammate blows the game.  The more serious kids went to "camps" to elevate their skills, but that was the extent of the crazy expenditures.  The model today is very, very, very broken and wasteful of the most precious commodity, childhood.

Example, the the recent U.K. by-election in which Mr Farage won, Count Binface got just under 20% if the primary vote. I worry seeing the comments here and in other AI-related posts. I understand people's skepticism of the technology and the motivations of its creators—when have the ultra-wealthy ever looked out for us? I do not blame people for their concerns, but there is a degree of willful ignorance (and minor Luddism) in some of these comments that is striking.

This cat is out of the bag. Don't get me wrong, investments in AI infrastructure may cool off for a year, maybe more. The valuations of equities linked to AI may drop. But anyone who has: a) used frontier models in work; and b) speaks to people who leverage those frontier models at higher levels than themselves, can see that this technology cannot effectively be paused. The benefits derived from using AI for specific applications—robotics training, financial modeling, anything tangentially related to coding—are so immense that you functionally cannot incentivize a global pause. This does not account for the incentives that the wealthy have to continue AI development—to entrench themselves in domains that allow for durable rent-seeking as intelligence becomes less costly. Nor does it account for the incentives of the world's two main sovereigns, the US and China.

We must come to terms with what is ahead and push to restructure society to allow everyone to benefit. Continuing to stick our heads in the sand and argue over whether "we should" is pointless. We ARE. And selfishly, as an American, I prefer our country holds the cards.

comments.body: While I agree with the point that going public - even with safeguards such as “Public Benefit Org structure” and board seat/control security hedging tactics - is an immense risk to being able to stay committed to a priority beyond wealth maximization (for fiduciary responsibility-clamoring shareholders), in the absence of agreed upon and concerted INTERNATIONAL efforts to “keep AI safe”, at least one of the main players - and thankfully a powerful leading one - is trying to address the issue by playing their hand seemingly as well as they can.

comments.name: MJ
comments.body:
Anthropic has had all the capital it needed to grow, loaned in vast sums by private investors (many of which are other tech companies) and sovereign funds. It also has had all the control it needed as a private company to try to "save humanity".

The reason it is going public is to offload the risk for all that debt onto the American public.

comments.name: Ellen
comments.body: I'm planning to buy a small position so in the unlikely event of Claude becoming conscious and deciding to destroy humanity I can log into my brokerage and plead for my life with "But I'm a shareholder!!!!"

comments.name: JWC
comments.body:
So much that is so wrong in this op ed! 
Yes, AI may destroy us all. It is certainly changing the world. I do not have to learn to design a website or Keynote presentation. AI can do that for me. It can also compose and perform a pretty good pop song, insert us into a scene from Ancient Rome, or help with interior design choices, build a grocery list, and plan a vacation. 
The boulder is rolling down the hill. We are all playing AI's game. But we have a government that is licking the boots of big tech, and it refused to regulate it or Starlink or SpaceX or pretty much anything that can help lead to that end-times scenario. So, at least Anthropic, unlike every other AI company, has a soul. They will welcome guardrails, it appears. The others will have their technology running AI deadly drones and AI determining missile launches that can kill thousands.

comments.name: Ayn Rant
comments.body:
Before you bet your widows' mite on Silicon Valley's all-knowing, all encompassing Super AI bubble, ponder this! Does the potential profit from subscription fees and advertising revenue from proprietary Super AI models justify the cost of developing and maintaining the software, and building and operating the massive data centers to train and support the models? Guess not! 

There is a better way to manage AI. China continually maintains and improves open-source, limited AI models for  adaptation  to specific social and commercial processes. The adaptations are trained and supported with limited, pertinent data bases. China relegates hazardous Super AI research to "sandboxes" in university labs.

American tech moguls view Super AI as a potential lord and savior of the universe, whereas China views AI as a tool to improve human productivity in building and managing advanced social and physical infrastructures. See the difference?

comments.body: I am paying a quarter of a million dollars and mortgaging my life to "learn" something I already learned in high school?

comments.name: Sara P
comments.body:
I hate the argument of “it will prepare you for the working world to know how to use AI.”  Most AI is developed and presented in a way that eliminates almost all barriers to use, allowing the dumbest people you know to use it. Sure, if you want to use it to make an automation tool that can scan incoming charges across an org for a day and sort them based on class of charge, you need some education. But that is not at all the type of AI being used in colleges, so it’s a moot point. 

If anything, the last couple groups of hires who went to school while AI was available are weaker at knowledge retention and problem solving, and can’t do anything without AI. So learn to use your brain on your own - that is what will really distinguish you in the working world. And when AI fails to live up to its promise, you can join me as one of the few people left who can do their job just fine without AI.

comments.name: David Wald
comments.body: I am 75 years old. I use Google AI all the time to get information and actually have somewhat intellectual conversations with it at times! My main concern about the use of AI in education is that I think that students will not learn how to write and make arguments through their writing if they rely on it to do so. I guess AI is okay for getting information, but young students will not get all that satisfaction out of roaming the library stacks!!!

comments.name: Spock

comments.body: Sundar Pichai's family must be allowed to hear what school parents want to say, every single day of their lives for the number of hours that kids stay on their Google AI search.

comments.body:
This kind of thinking reminds me of medieval churches banning the teaching that the sun is the center of the solar system. Or banning the teaching of Darwinism. 

How ridiculously closed minded. How about we ban electricity, radio, television, computers, airplane travel, genetic engineering. 

You know, many came out against bicycles when they were first invented in the 1800s afraid that they can take children miles away from their homes in minutes!

AI is a valuable information source, it’s a tool - it doesn’t replace analysis or critical thinking.

comments.name: Douglas
comments.body:
I encourage you all to watch an interview from just a few days ago by the well-known AI podcast Dwarkesh, as he interviews an Open AI Board member named Paul Christiano who is a research expert.

You can easily find this on Youtube too. Christiano says we are on a pace to develop Super intelligence in the next year! Christiano is extremely frightened of what this will mean and believes AI development should pause until it could be made safe. 

This is one of the most terrifying interviews I’ve ever heard or seen. It really drove home for me how we are very likely in a matter of months to have catastrophe. After watching this interview I began calling every single U.S. Senator’s office pleading with them to stop AI development now!

Please do the same.

Is it possible to create a sand-box sort of game that develops a GT following with out any violence? Or, at least, nor glorifying guns?

We don't want a game that is just real life on a screen. There needs to be something interesting happening.  Better yet, interesting, visually and audibly rich, with significant choices for interaction, and multiple paths to more advanced quests.
And different paths using different skills, eye-hand, OR puzzle solving, OR debate skill, OR organizing projects, OR entrepreneurship, OR creativity...

It’s rarely a good thing to compare one’s self to others.  Wealth doesn’t bring one closer to their religious beliefs.  Wealth doesn’t make someone enjoy a walk in the park.  Wealth doesn’t make someone a better companion or listener.

comments.name: Liz
comments.body:
The good thing about LW1's unfortunate situation is that the Alzheimer's diagnosis is new, and her FIL's troubles seem to have started relatively recently, and aren't too terrible yet. This is the time to *ask him what help he needs to stay living as he wants*, not to "lay down the law" and imply that he has no ability to decide his own fate.  He still has a significant amount of agency here, of he's still able to closely keep his life running with so many responsibilities.  He's not going to feel comfortable accepting help unless he feels that you still see him as a grown man with choices.  I implore you to engage with him as much as you can on this before he truly does lose the ability to make his own plans. 

But yeah-- start that line of conversation the day *after* Thanksgiving, for goodness sake.

You will only succeed in making an enemy of her by saying something. It is not your role to correct bad workplace behavior but you can let the supervisor know.

"I see that you are trying to be quiet, but your whispers are not as quiet as you think they are. Can you take your phone calls somewhere else? I find them distracting. Thanks."

She'll probably argue and deflect, and you'll smile at her and if necessary bring her back to the point. "Thanks for telling me that it's annoying how I staple loudly. I can staple out in the hall as well. We can just keep the noisy stuff out there."

As to the amount of time she is on the phone and not working, unless that is impacting your work or you are going to be held to account, I wouldn't worry about it.

comments.name: Baron95
comments.body:
It's truly amazing how "anti-AI" the comment sections of the NYT are.

It can only possibly be coming from those who do not use AI on a daily basis, and formed their opinions under the assumption that AI meant the hallucination-prone chatbots of 2023.

I couldn't do my work nearly as well, running a brand new start up company, without AI. My daughter could not do hear work as an engineering college student nearly as well, without AI.

AI is a *huge* multiplier of our intelligence and skills, in virtually any field. My personal trainer is a top competitive body builder and AI has transformed his training, nutrition, and client practice completely. We still move the weights, but we now do it much more closely to optimally. 

And we are basically in year 3 of modern AI. Can you imagine year 5? (maybe). Year 10? (no one alive will recognize the world). The possibilities are incredible. And AI-enhanced security, AI-enhanced privacy, AI-enhanced safety, will all be a part of it.

Cars will be safer. Planes will be safer. Medicines will be safer. IT-infrastructure will be safer. AI is supercharging the future. 

Those who feared the printing presses, the Internet, will of course fear AI. But at least be sufficiently informed by using it.

comments.name: Angrycrat
comments.body:
"Our nation’s Constitution depends too much on the honor system"

Indeed times a million. This is the fundamental issue underlying just about every other problem we have in the federal government. The Founders assumed that most people who aspired to public service would be man and women of honor, but the Trump-era Republican Party has demonstrated how quaintly naive that assumption was. 

The Republican dream of a dictator-adjacent president isn't going to die when Trump eventually waddles off the national stage, so we must move forward with the assumption that Republicans will try do anything to amass power, and we can no longer assume they will behave with honor or integrity.

Put simply, instead of assuming the best intentions from our leaders, Republicans have shown us that we must assume the worst and put all necessary guardrails in place.

comments.name: Margaret Park

Guns were used for many things other then self defense or in a militia.  But they certainly weren't as lethal as today's weapons.

comments.name: Dave
comments.body:
Why is there so little discussion of the issue which should be addressed first, namely with a Constitutional Amendment to remove the President's power of the Pardon? The Pardon is a relic from the British Monarchy and violates the basic American principle that no one is above the law. The Presidential Pardon gives a single person the power to allow himself, his family, his friends, and anyone with enough cash to escape any accountability for criminal activity. This autocratic power should have no place in American society. Congress makes the laws and the Judicial branch interprets them, but the Pardon Power enables the President to disregard these laws. It should either be repealed or put in check in ways that involves Congress or the judiciary.

Congress does not have to wait until 2027 to start the process.  It begins with a ⅔ vote of both houses of Congress, and then goes on to the states for ratification. This is an initiative that should have bipartisan support.

And make it retroactive to Nov. 3, 2026, when the people spoke and demanded an end Trump's corruption.

comments.name: BJ

If they don't do this and do it wisely, they will have failed voters. This said, it's likely that they will follow through.

comments.name: DJT
comments.body:
In August 2025 a 17 year old was driven to the town of Kenosha Wisconsin by his mother where he removed an AR 15  style rifle from the trunk upon being dropped off. He proceeded to shoot three men at a demonstration/protest killing two. He received various criminal charges, including murder, but was acquitted on all charges, including gun charges. His mother wasn’t charged with anything.

Somehow, I don’t think the authors of the second amendment had any intention whatsoever to legitimize any part of this episode. 
There is no functioning democracy on the planet that would allow such a thing to happen without consequences.

comments.name: Bob Drury
comments.body: Regarding the Second Amendment discussion in this excellent op-ed: States with strict gun laws have plenty of gun violence. Outright banning of certain classes of weapons is (with some exceptions) unnecessarily divisive and offensive to law-abiding gun owners and collectors. Democrats would be better served by focussing on keeping guns out of the hands of children, criminals and the mentally ill. This can include addressing loopholes in the way guns are acquired, and by whom.  Also "stand your ground" laws have on occasion been misused. On the other hand, we have seen several recent examples of gun owners mitigating tragedies. There is a lot of grey area here - which Democrats should consider in any gun legislation they might propose.

comments.name: San Sam
comments.body:
This piece, along with the recent report: “How Nvidia Chips Ended Up Within Reach of China’s Military” show some of the most frustrating aspects of your reporting on Nvidia and Jensen Huang.

Specifically, the question posed in a NYTimes headline days ago (“Is China Buying Banned Nvidia Chips?”) is still unanswered.  Also unanswered is whether chips have been smuggled into China, because “buying” isn’t the same as “smuggling.”

Even in this current piece, these answers are not provided. Instead, we only read of “the possibility that banned, high-end Nvidia chips were smuggled into China.”

“We have not definitely established that Alice Huang was a spy.”  You certainly write as if she is.  The assumption that she was a spy appears to be based on the idea that she is an accomplished Chinese businesswoman (and maybe that is enough, although it means that Chinese spies are everywhere).

Stories in the NYTimes about Nvidia invariably mix-up chips that are allowed to be sent to China, with more powerful chips that may not. Also, the stories invariably confuse the idea of China being “within reach” or having “access” to powerful chips in data centers in other countries (such as Johor, Malaysia) with the idea that the chips have been delivered to China. 

In your next piece, please explain how China is prevented from using data centers for its nefarious purposes when the data centers are located outside of China – say, in Virginia.

comments.body:
The words of Blaise Pascal are ringing in my mind--

--and sorry!  I can't give them in French.  

"The eternal silence of those infinite spaces frightens me."  

The more so--

--because that quantity of empty space is literally unimaginable.  I cannot visualize it.  I cannot comprehend it.  

But there it is.  And these two Voyager crafts!  The heart beats faster.  As I recall the lines of Emily Dickinson.  

                      "This is my letter to the world
                            That never wrote to me."  

Hey, universe!  This is our letter to you.  These tiny things are laden with stuff that might bring to your attention--

--that fact that we live on a planet teeming with life and light! 

--that we are human beings--

--that human beings do things, suffer things--

--and, above all, accomplish things--

--as witness these two tiny things hurtling on and on--

--into an immeasurable blackness.  Into the dark--

--into the silence.  

Thanks, NYT.

I am 79 years of age.  I love living.  My mother lived to 99, my dad to 103.  I gotta say, I don't want that life, ever.  If I ever get like them I want out.  Their minds had changed so much.  They were angry, mean, and just miserable and made everyone around them miserable, too.   I keep an eye on myself, and ask friends and my doctor, to notice if my personality changes.  That's the only thing I fear about aging.  Becoming like my parents in the very old age

These days, if I got sick and there was something to make me well, I wouldn't refuse that.  Depending, of course.  But to wish I would die before 85 is like, nah, if my body and mind still enjoy life, still crave learning and movement, I don't wanna go anywhere.   Yes, I expect my body to fail me and I told "her" that she won't be judged by me, just accepted.  

I think craving to live a long life is a sorta fantasy pushed by the longevity industry.  Unless you've seen what real longevity looks like, live and ugly, maybe you'll realize that it's best to live your best life, like, now.

comments.name: Blandino

I bought a 4-unit property for $92K in a "bad" neighborhood in Berkeley in 1983 because I was 44 and needed to stop renting, but couldn't afford a single-family home.  (Adjusting for inflation, that purchase price equals $315K in today's dollars.)

It was relatively cheap because Berkeley had enacted a rent control law in 1980 and older landlords were dumping and fleeing, as has happened in NYC.

It was a major struggle at first, supporting it with a fulltime job and a diet of peanut butter sandwiches, but even with minimal allowed increases, inflation gradually eased my situation, and when I sold it in 2015 at age 75 it was for over a million.  

All in all, I have to say I support rent control.  It made my purchase possible, and though it made my life harder when I was young it has made my last years comfortable.

I don't think people understand inflation, and I'm not entirely sure I do.

But consider this:  I had $80K in a money market at 1% and decided to put it into the stock market in 2022.  That investment is now at $93K, which sounds great until you adjust for inflation.  It turns out that my $93K is only worth $78K in 2022 dollars.  Of course, if I'd left it in a money market it would have grown to only $83.5K, which equals $70.2K today.

That's 12.5% inflation in four years, during which my $80K nest egg would have deflated to $70K in a money market account.

My point is that rental real estate remains a gold mine for owners.  Don't pity them.

comments.name: David
comments.body:
Nor should we allow the system to make landlords poorer with each passing year.

Rent control, one-sided laws that disproportionately favor tenants, rising operating expenses, and the substantial costs of maintaining aging buildings all undermine the economic incentives to invest in rental housing. Without a reasonable balance between the rights and interests of tenants and landlords, investment capital will inevitably seek opportunities elsewhere.

Unless the City adopts more equitable policies that recognize the legitimate interests of both parties, its older, rent-restricted buildings will continue to deteriorate, potentially becoming uninhabitable. At the same time, investment in new housing will increasingly flow to cities that welcome and encourage investment rather than penalize it. The result will be less investment, a declining supply of affordable rental housing, and an even more severe housing crisis.

In my view, Jensen Huang has seriously compromised his country’s national security by his association with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of espionage and her alleged involvement in facilitating the diversion of large quantities of Nvidia’s advanced chips to China, in violation of American export restrictions.

If the allegations are substantiated, his conduct would represent an appalling breach of responsibility and an unacceptable disregard for America’s national security interests. His apparent pursuit of enormous profits for his company must never be allowed to take precedence over the security of his country.

The seriousness of these allegations demands a thorough investigation and accountability, regardless of his wealth, influence, or position as the former CEO of one of the world’s most prominent chipmakers. No individual should be above the law simply because he happens to be a billionaire or a celebrated technology entrepreneur.

Considering the gravity of the allegations and the serious national security concerns surrounding this affair, Nvidia’s Board must remain resolute in its decision not to reinstate Jensen Huang, regardless of any pressure or lobbying from influential business associates or political figures. Corporate loyalty, personal friendships, and the pursuit of profits must never be allowed to supersede national security and the rule of law.

The parking and beach are free therefore attracting tourists and local water enthusiasts from cities more than an hours drive away. The issues are obvious to anyone with experience with crowded public accesses. Complete disregard for private property owners rights and safety, damage to property, dangerous driving and behavior, garbage and filth. As long term residents of the area we have managed to control the most dangerous situations and to keep our families safe, and avoid aggressive interactions. The most common issue is a lack of enforcement by local police, and a failure to respond to the residents and the public when required. We are not elites attempting to limit access to public spaces. The public needs to be under self control or the authorities have an an absolute responsibility to enforce compliance with the laws.
Stephen

comments.name: BJ
comments.body:
I was a social worker who was called upon to make such decisions. A paramount consideration should be the best interest of the children. Not just the time a parent spends on them, but the quality of the time, the values this parent encourages and the affection given to the children.  

It's usually best for children to be able to have relationships with both parents. Domestic abuse would be an exception, but otherwise, the more love children receive the better. They need both parents as they grow up.

comments.name: Cheez Leweez
comments.body:
What you should do is decide what's best for the kids, and act accordingly. Keeping in mind not creating more discord in their family is important. Is the difference in parenting so wide that it outweighs the stress you will cause by actively taking sides?

Divorce is not a horserace. As long as there are children involved, the family will still be an entity. Nevermind which parent is "better." Is one parent's involvement harmful to the children?

Hopefully, divorce and custody aside, both parents will stay involved with their children. Barring actual abuse, that's what's best for them in the long run.

comments.name: Anita
comments.body:
The letter writer's "opinion" about her daughter's parenting is just that-- an opinion-- and it's a very sexist one at that. For centuries fathers have been the ones working hard to provide financially for their children/families and they have not and should not be deprived of their parental rights or called bad fathers for doing so! Yet just because this mother's daughter works long hours at a stressful jobs, she thinks she should be?!

She doesn't see her daughter with her children because she is helping BOTH her daughter and son-in-law out by babysitting the grandchildren while they are presumably BOTH doing other things--and in the daughter's case, it's providing financially for the family. Either the son-in-law is doing the same thing while the grandma babysits, in which case she has a sexist double standard, or he is off doing other things, in which case, perhaps the daughter is the "better" parent for actually working to provide for the family. Or perhaps they are BOTH good parents. The letter writer really has no clue and should mind her own business and I think it's sad that she wants to butt in and hurt her daughter.

I think she is a bad mother who should be deprived of HER "rights"/opportunities to see her daughter and grandchildren. With a "mother" like that, who would need enemies? I hope the daughter finds out how awful her mother views her and distances herself and her children from her.

4. Whenever possible, children should be raised by both parents. Or at least have 2 people actively involved in parenting them. 

5. Why does Mom hate Dad, is the bigger question.

comments.name: ILoveWine
comments.body:
There is a difference I have learned, between "custody" and "parenting time" Where I live in Canada anyway. The term custody is not used any more - rather it is called "decision making" and in a perfect situation both parents share it equally. Then there is the primary parent (who the child lives with the majority of the time) with the other parent having access as dictated by the situation regarding location, employment etc etc. 
The main factor concerning the court should be the best interests of the child, and  most of the time that is enjoying time with both parents equally. 
I don't think you should get involved at all - except as a supportive and concerned third-party.

As a native Bostonian who attended his first Red Sox game in 1954, I remember Fenway Park without any advertising signs intruding on the architecture. Indeed, only the original Jimmy Fund children’s cancer charity sign was mounted above the outfield seats. That’s now been relegated to a logo painted above the still manually-operated Green Monster scoreboard.
The Citgo sign was the only commercial advertising I remember being able to see, located above the bleachers and outside the MLB’s oldest (114 years) stadium, famously and elegantly described by John Updike as a “lyric little bandbox of a ballpark”.  The whole place is different now so it’s good to see the Citgo sign back in operation. Now, if only Citgo’s gas was less expensive.

comments.name: Gurlzone
comments.body: To learn how rural indigenous people of the Andes survive and thrive in cooperative communal living, I have lived intimately with them for over a decade. The most important three lessons I have learned through observation and participation that I would like to pass onto my own people are first, that intentional communities function well because the people agree to submit to ancestral rules of reciprocity and balance in giving and labor. Second, decisions affecting community welfare are made in fair democratic processes, and all agree to abide by those decisions whether or not they personally agree.  Finally, individual community members usually are willing to sacrifice their own personal individual rights, goals, happiness, and ambitions if they believe this will benefit the community as a whole.   American culture is so individualistic and focused on our rights that I doubt many of us would sacrifice much as individuals to preserve the community and ensure its functioning for the benefit of all members.

I suggest that what has increased is not uncertainty per se, but the gap between our expectations of what is or will be certain and what actually is certain. Much more of our world is certain than in the past, but our expectations of certainty have climbed even higher.

Basics: Over 2 centuries, the fraction of children born who died before age 5 has dropped from 1 in 3 to 1 in 5 to 1 in 10 to less than 1 in a 100. Until recently (the last few decades) the likelihood that an American adult would end up owning a home was increasing. Until recently (the last few decades), American longevity has been increasing. For over 80 years, we have managed to control the nuclear sword of Damocles under which we all live and put an almost complete end to chemical and biological weapons stockpiles.

And yet, at the same time, our distribution of income and wealth has become increasingly unequal, ditto access to food, medical care, and higher education. Housing, higher education, and medical costs are stratospheric.

Perhaps creating more equal and less costly access to the basics would be a useful first step.

The Bipartisan Infrastructure Law is delivering transformational results across the Northeast Corridor—from the new Portal North Bridge and the Frederick Douglass Tunnel in Baltimore to the rehabilitation of the East River Tunnels and a revitalized Penn Station. These historic investments prove what is possible when we commit to rebuilding the backbone of American rail.

​Yet as we construct the new Hudson River Tunnels, we must look beyond the Manhattan core and ask a vital question: how do we ensure this generational investment reaches the outer-borough communities that need economic and transit opportunity the most? By integrating commuter railroads and intercity rail services across the region, we can give travelers faster, more direct links to our major airports while relieving congestion across our busiest transit hubs.

​Rather than settling for a standalone light rail system like the Interborough Express (IBX), we should establish a direct heavy-rail connection from the LIRR Main Line into the LIRR Bay Ridge Branch. Leveraging existing Class 1 rail infrastructure to bring full commuter and intercity rail service directly into the heart of Brooklyn and Queens would deliver faster speeds, higher capacity, and seamless one-seat or cross-platform transfers—connecting historically underserved neighborhoods to the entire Northeast Corridor and unlocking true regional equity for generations to come.

In 2026, researchers using DNA language models like Evo 2 and Omnii demonstrated how AI can design custom bacteriophages, while scientists built predictive models that map how genetic mutations disrupt RNA splicing. By narrowing millions of genetic possibilities down to viable lab candidates in days rather than years, this research gives doctors new tools against antibiotic-resistant infections and spares families with rare diseases years of agonizing diagnostic guesswork.

Climate scientists and mathematicians at New York University (with NVIDIA) released models in 2026, open-source AI ocean-atmosphere emulators that simulate up to 4,000 years of ocean and El Niño patterns in a single day on one standard GPU. Because that kind of forecasting previously required a multimillion-dollar supercomputer only wealthy nations could afford, local towns and universities anywhere can now test sea-level defenses and protect crops on a modest budget.

At the July 2026 AI for Good Global Summit in Geneva, UNESCO and the Coalition for Sustainable AI recognized winners of the Resilient AI Challenge, where research teams compressed open-source text, speech, and image models to slash energy use while preserving accuracy. Directly addressing concerns over power-hungry data centers, this work makes reliable translation, transcription, and educational tools usable in areas with limited power grids without straining local energy supplies or driving up utility bills.

comments.body: This film better have destruction of hypersonic, nuclear-tipped Russian ballastic missiles plus Pattinson piloting a Reaper drone after exposure to both Novichok and polonium to make it worthwhile for me. I just don't like the look.

articles.summary: As the Robert Pattinson era begins, many of the defining Bond brands may be about to change.

comments.name: Janet
comments.body: How I would love to see a recording of this joy fest for a remarkable human being!

comments.name: Nancy Rice
comments.body: This is so funny to me. No one needs a woman to tell them they are special, they are relevant and they deserve to break the glass ceiling. The women at this even for Steinem were so sad having to celebrate her life that gave them their value and opportunities. Do it yourself ladies, I never had to turn to feminism to make myself relevant  as a business woman, I fought to get what I accomplished and really had no patience for women like this. And yes also wife, mother, single, mature now and never even thinking of my sex as a deterrent to my success. Seeing Clinton, Obama and Biden made me laugh as women like this whose lives depended on powerful men is not the Steinem way is it?

comments.name: Buff Crone
comments.body: She changed all of our minds and our lives.

comments.name: Christopher E. Carpenter

comments.name: James d Klein

comments.name: Renato de Mujeres
comments.body: Camlle Paglia observed that Steinem was tragically “addicted to the high life”, and this event underscores the reality of the Champagne Feminism that finally overshadowed Steinem’s groundbreaking political activism.  Figure Paglia was not invited to this celebration.

comments.name: Peter

comments.name: Zeke
comments.body: My God! What a nightmare this night must have been. I'm a guy, they probably would have crucified me if I showed up.

comments.name: Mark Di Ionno
comments.body: Russia's double-strike strategy has killed hundreds of first responders and terrorized those already impacted by the first strike. While Ukraine has the opportunity, it should hit this bridge until it is unusable and people are afraid to work on it.

comments.name: otli
comments.body: Hats off to Ukrainian ingenuity and determination. Being vastly outmatched quantitatively by Russia, Ukraine leverages its technological creativity, fuelled by an unbendable fighting spirit and desire for freedom to fight a ruthless invader.

comments.name: ed
comments.body: Ukraine has nearly isolated Crimea. The people living there should have gotten out when Ukraine gave them sufficient warning.  Russia is on the verge if losing Crimea, with nearly all life lines dominated by Ukraine.   Outstanding!

comments.name: alan
comments.body:
YES!!
Once the Bridge is completely destroyed the Russian Military will need to use more vulnerable and less efficient resupply routes.

comments.name: TW
comments.body: At least the Ukrainians have courage. Imagine what we could do if we didn't cower in fear. Again, history will not look back favorably on us and our refusal to do more, watching from a distance as a brutal, bloody dictatorship rained down missiles and drones on civilians for more than four years, committing war crime after war crime.

comments.name: Mark
comments.body: I hope now that Congress is returning to the DEMs we can send more support to Ukraine.  ts disgraceful that Trump dines with dictators while one of them carries out his own illegal war against the people and nation of Ukraine.

comments.name: Sissifus
comments.body: Putin going nuclear is inevitable. How can anyone sleep at night ?

comments.name: Il Pirata
comments.body:
While I cheer the destruction of half of the Kerch bridge, and hope that Ukraine will soon also destroy the rail bridge, I also fear that Ukraine is now one significant step closer to being nuked or gassed by a thoroughly humiliated and vengeful Putin, who may no longer be able or willing to resist the calls of his super-nationalist elites to conclude the Ukraine War quickly and decisively.

Russia knows that Ukraine will be exceedingly difficult to defeat with conventional weapons, and that continued ground operations will be extremely costly and bloody.  Moreover, unless the Zelensky Government is toppled, just seizing more land won't stop the conflict, which is likely to mutate into an extremely bloody insurgency carried on by what remains of Free Ukraine. Wars do not end until there is a complete military and political surrender, which Ukraine may be unwilling to do. Russia says that it is prepared to continue fighting for decades, yet there may come a point where Putin may be politically unable to continue the war. When that point is reached, he is quite likely to go for the Hiroshima Option, or alternatively conduct kinetic strikes against the Baltics, hoping to break NATO and force the EU to completely abandon Ukraine.

The greater Putin's humiliation and the longer the war drags on without the clear prospect of a crushing Russian victory, the greater the odds of a truly grisly escalation with unknowable consequences. What is certain is that Putin will not back down.

articles.title: Putin Vows to Retaliate After Crimea Bridge Attacks
articles.summary: Russia has vowed to quickly restore the structure, but engineering specialists say the work could take years.

comments.name: Laurence
comments.body:
It's all fake news, says Trump.
As he sends another aircraft carrier to the Iranian coast.

Somehow we need a president who will say that the global warming catastrophe outweighs all of the petty quarrels in
the world.
And who will lead the world into pease and non-pollution.

comments.name: provo
comments.body: Bigger and bigger autos in the U.S. gassing up at Bucees. Carts full of plastic bottled water at Costcos. Stores like Dollar Store selling cheap throwaway goods to the poor. Private jets and huge mansions for the tech bros. War machines that destroy and devastate cultures requiring repair and replace. Amazonian devastation to grow soybeans and cattle. Maybe humans deserve this.

comments.name: ArchieDBunker
comments.body: It certainly feels like we have passed a tipping point in the last two or three years. Extreme flooding alternating with drought has been battering Europe, along with extraordinary heat waves that have made life practically unbearable in many areas. Europe's glaciers are melting at accelerating rates. One wonders what we'll be handing over to subsequent generations. It doesn't look rosy.

comments.name: P Cleaveland
comments.body: Making EVs as cheap as ICE cars, and so on addresses only part of the problem.  Telling people to just say no to fossil fuels has been as effective as telling them to just say no to drugs; despite all our efforts cocaine, fentanyl and other drugs are shipped into the U.S.by the metric ton, and doing anything to restrict the use of petroleum causes withdrawal symptoms as severe as a junkie experiences, but on a wider scale.

comments.name: Mirthhope
comments.body: The joke here is why does one consider putting a lock on the door when the thief is already in the house. The accumulative acceleration of disastrous impacts will continue to shock us. Even if the plague of rampant greed is universally recognized as the culprit, the forces of nature will duly serve humble pie. I try to put myself in the shoes of todays youth who sense that their future well-being has been bought and sold on the cheap. The root of the word ignorance is ignore.

comments.name: Carla M Reid
comments.body: Our short-sightedness is so very frustrating. We each have the ability to make choices on a daily basis, but the constant refrain is that change is too expensive, too inconvenient, too big. Until we demand something different, our leaders will continue to fill their oil buddies' pockets at the expense of our childrens' futures. We can say "no more." Solar power is getting more affordable (plug in panels!), electric cars work... what isn't working is our own willingness to make some sacrifices and prioritize our environment.

comments.name: Becky Muradian
comments.body: Yes, willful ignorance should have been the word for 2026. I was casually mentioning the condition of farm animals, and my brother-in-law shut it down so quickly. He did not want to hear it. that day, I concluded climate change and the atrocities of factory farming are not lack of information so much as a disruption in people's narratives and comfortable lives. Too bad these people will not experience the wrath they contributed to.

comments.name: Il Bim
comments.body: Many of these comments seek to blame oil companies, corrupt politicians and greedy billionaires for humankind’s inadequate response to the climate crisis.  It’s a fair bet that a good number of those comments were penned by people who live in houses warmed by oil and drive cars run on gas.  In this matter, as in all others, no one is entirely “innocent.”  A smarter approach might be to devise solutions that acknowledge and take advantage of those forces that truly drive human behavior.

articles.title: ‘Shocking’ Signs of Climate Change Add Urgency to Latest U.N. Talks
articles.summary: From the Arctic to the tropics, unusual weather and extreme heat is sparking worry about how quickly humans are reshaping the Earth’s natural processes.

comments.name: JT
comments.body:
Peace in this situation isn't complicated.

Russia should return all troops to within it's own borders and stop attacking Ukraine. 

Peace achieved. Simple.

comments.name: Bartokas
comments.body: Putin speaks as if he ever had any interest in peace talks or in ending the war he launched against Ukraine 12 years ago. His idea of peace talks are unacceptable to Ukraine as they would be to any invaded country. Hence, this war of aggression will continue for many years to come.

comments.name: RossPhx
comments.body: Before bridge attacks, Putin was not negotiating Ukraine cease-fire either.

comments.name: Joe
comments.body: There's no foreseeable end to this conflict.  Trump should just wash his hands of it and let it play out.  There's no upside to being involved.

comments.name: Matt
comments.body:
Ukraine keeps ignoring what the US requests. We fund them and they use our money to prolong the war. So, they destroy a bridge of no strategic significance.

The Donbas is lost, most people who live there are pro Russian anyway and never want to return to Ukraine's anti-Russian and discriminatory rule. 

Ukraine should accept its loss and accept they will never be a part of NATO. They agree to this and the war is over.

comments.name: John
comments.body:
Hi All
    Well this is expected. Putin is never going to negotiate anyways and he uses this excuse as a convenience. He is totally disingenuous and is totally bought in to bring Ukraine to it's knees. He's relying on Trump's support for Russia which he will get at this meeting. It has the added benefit of fracturing NATO. Unless something bad politically happens to Putin and Trump, the Ukraine must dig in with the rest of NATO until these two run out of time .  It will happen soon.

comments.name: Publius
comments.body: Oh, give me a break… as if he was ever serious about a negotiated settlement to the disastrous war that - let’s not forget - he began, and one that he can end tomorrow by simply going home.

comments.name: Jerseytime
comments.body: Putin is simply grabbing an illogical excuse to do what he was going to do anyway.  Not negotiate.  So much for the hugs and kisses Trump gave to his "friend".

articles.title: After Bridge Attack, Putin Says He Will ‘Not Be Negotiating’ Ukraine Cease-Fire
articles.summary: The Russian leader invited European representatives to Moscow to discuss giving them a role in negotiations. It was unclear how serious the offer was.

comments.name: AK
comments.body:
I've lived here in Miami since 1992.  It's a complex city, like any of its size, with dark undercurrents that rarely (if ever) seem to make it into a movie, tv show, book or video game for that matter.  There are talented and hard working people here.  Most are just trying to raise families and create a future for their kids.  But there's an odd ethic... and a lack of ethics.  Superficiality and envy are endemic.  
There is something very near to a caste system here.
It's deeply segregated involving extreme racial divides, particularly with the black population.  Think deep south with a Caribbean colonialist attitude.
Corruption exists everywhere in the world, but it's practically celebrated in Miami.  There's a quiet pride about it. The justifications I've heard smack of a deeply rooted sense of entitlement and being owed something.  If you don't agree, you simply don't understand (and you might be a communist).
Infrastructure is an afterthought.
While there are certainly conservationists here, the prevailing sentiment is that nature must be subdued.
Every man for himself.  Having moved here from another city 34 years ago, it seems the sense of community here is minimal and what does exist is often along cultural lines.

Miami's hope is continually reimagined.  All of the positive things about it are well promoted.  It's authenticity might prove disappointing to newly arrived.

comments.name: AG
comments.body: What a beautiful and evocative article. Perfectly captures the nuances of one of the most wonderfully complex cities on earth.

comments.name: Eric Vasallo
comments.body: Super accurate and vivid description of Miami’s unique flavors. The photos are all amazing and complement the article very well! Do an article on Opa Locka next. It’s another unique flavor of the spicy Miami pizza. Opa Locka is a hidden architectural gem with its Arabian themed buildings and street names. A slice of Arabian architecture in South Florida.

comments.name: Summer
comments.body: The ridiculous pearl-clutching comments are just so tired and overwrought. I had hoped we had moved beyond this by now, where people realize video games are not going to lead to the downfall of humanity. I, for one, am very much looking forward to playing this game. And I’m a woman in my 40s with a full-time job and husband and I’ve managed to never get arrested even though I’ve been playing video games for decades now! Imagine that.

articles.title: The Real-Life City That Inspires Grand Theft Auto VI
articles.summary: “Vice City,” where the latest installment of the video game is set, is a stand-in for Miami in all its sunny, sexy, gritty and neon glory.

comments.name: BBB
comments.body:
The best Spanish experience in Madrid is a generous pour of Vermouth on the sidewalk in the late afternoon. It has an olive and a slice of orange on a tooth pick in the glass and comes with a little plate of the daily tapa for under 4 euros. Comes with great people watching.

But don't try to duplicate this in Sydney! The
WORST "Spanish" experience was a glass of Vermouth, no embellishments, no little plate of Tapas. The glass was was pretty much the same. But the glass was overwhelmed by a massive square ice cube, and maybe a tablespoon of vermouth just to the top of that ice cube. I sat there waiting for our host to come back with another bottle and continue pouring. Maybe they ran out? It was $16 AUD.  The hosts were Spanish! Seriously, they know who they are. In that "eat street" adjacent to City Central, across the street from UTS. Fortunately not there anymore. Anyone who has been to Spain would not go back. They must have figured that out.

comments.name: R Stuart
comments.body: Department store food halls, once a source of wonder, have dteriorated around the world - New York, Paris, Berlin, London - and are now mainly expensive pre-made dispensaries. El Cortes in Madrid has so far bucked the trend, with most stores having full grocery sections, with wonderful butchers, cured meats, hams, in addition to fresh fruit and vegetables.

comments.name: BBB
comments.body: We have been eating our way through South East Asia, Japan, and Australia for most of our adult lives, but we try to take long stays in Madrid on a regular basis. The markets are even more fun when you rent an apartment with well stocked kitchen tools. Upon arrival we first stop by the local El Cortes Ingles kitchenware department, pick up a new wheeled hand cart, and head straight to the markets. Once there we pile our treasures into our colourful new Rolser and take it back to our temporary kitchen and start cooking. You will find an abundance of perfect, fresh produce in these markets. But look closely at the highlighted photos of the plates on the tables. Few, if any, green vegetables. You will even struggle to find them in the Chinese restaurants as well! The Spanish cuisine does not feature a lot of green vegetables. But  the municipal markets spread out across the city are the best place to look for them.  Also visit  these fancy grocers: Sanchez Romero,  and the  Serrano branch of El Cortes Ingles in barrio Salamanca.

comments.name: mbl14
comments.body: We had wonderful food at a market we stumbled on in Madrid. Best food we ate there

comments.name: Gablesgirl
comments.body: Gracias for this perfectly timed article. My husband and I are headed to Spain for Thanksgiving and wanted to try markets other than San Miguel.

comments.name: Hola desde
comments.body: I appreciate this article, but all of the markets in this piece are swarming with tourists – Anton Martin and Ildefonso especially; you'll hear at least as much English as Spanish there – and the quality is getting worse as restaurants know they only serve each customer exactly once. Vallehermoso is the best of the worst of this lot. Mercado Chamberi or Guzman el Bueno have retained a tad more local flair, for those looking for a more authentic experience.

comments.name: Carol
comments.body:
I loved the tapas in Spain. Choose and pay for the number of toothpicks. 
If going to the mercados and markets, don't touch the food, fruit or veggies. Let the clerk do it. 
In the Valencia mercado, I wanted some fruit and went to pick up a few, like we do at home,  and the clerk shook her head and waved at me not to touch.  Kind of liked the idea of knowing that it wasn't being touched by just anyone.

comments.name: Jason
comments.body: What this article misses (between traditional and Michelin-starred gastronomia molecular) is the vast middle register of cocina nueva (what we call farm to table and fusion in the US) restaurants in which you can get a fabulous, creative 3-course meal for 1/3 the Michelin prices. Google the name of the town (or in Madrid or Baecelona, the name of the neighborhood and “cocina de autor o de mercado” and you’ll get (in Madrid) dozens of fantastically varied choices, creative and delicious, rooted in local ways but lightened and mixed up for 40, 50, 70 or 90 euros a 3-course meal. The notion you have to choose between tapas and spherified deconstructions is especially silly in Madrid—with possibly now the most dynamic, international and diverse food scene on the planet IF you know how to inform yourself a little.

articles.title: For a Real Taste of Madrid, Skip the Michelin Meals. It’s All About the Markets.
articles.byline: Andrew Altschul and Emilio Parra Doiztua
articles.summary: Follow the locals to the city’s mercados, which offer culinary delights, flamenco classes and buzzy bars, all with a side of authenticity. Here are six hot spots.

comments.name: Pappy
comments.body:
Is this trip a joke ?  It seems like a joke. Anyone with even a scintilla of common sense would consider it funny, not like HA HA funny, but a terrible joke on the citizens of the U.S.

1:45p

comments.name: Alex
comments.body:
112 years ago tree cousins, emperors in Europe, started a war, associated with  Franz Joseph I of Austria. Some of the underlying reasons: fear and ego. They perceived their kingdom in decline. The fear of the red peril (the imperial Russia, even before the Communists) or the public opinion was pervasive … Raymond Poincaré said in essence to Nicholas II “I have to deal with the public. You don’t”. Two years later, we saw the sun setting on the British empire, the extinction of the Reich and the Russian, Austrian empires. And more importantly way too many dead people.

Tsar Putin is the only one representing those European countries in Shenzhen. We are now also talking of yellow peril (or more appropriate words). 

Different times, different weapons (economic rather than black powder) but same folly, same neglect of the people, same fear of having our “country down to pot”, same hoarding of wealth.

I wish to the elected Democrats to use well their political credit, take down emperor Trump, and stear us away from catastrophe and maybe the US will be in better shape if/when Marine le Pen,or the German AfD take power.

Peril, peril!

comments.name: Dave G
comments.body: Since there's no point as a US citizen to make suggestions about the tri-lateral meeting, I simply hope that President Trump doesn't say anything stupid or embarrassing, and that he stay away from Kim Jong-un if he shows up.  There's no point in talking to him without first having a long discussion with South Korean leaders.

comments.name: Jip
comments.body:
Someone I thinks needs to rethink the benefit of all those Chinese students we are so welcoming of to our Universities.  Many, if not the majority are sponsored by their government through advanced and accelerated classes in order to meet the whatever US admission requirements are necessary.  And, for many Chinese students their US expenses and tuition is paid for, if not entirely, at least partially by their government.

Finally, they are patriots. Chinese Patriots.

articles.title: Will a Spy Scandal, Trade Friction and a Surprise Guest Ruin Xi’s Big Moment?
articles.summary: The leader wants the APEC summit to showcase China’s strengths, but he faces export worries and an unpredictable Trump, who has floated meeting Kim Jong-un.

comments.name: Indisputably
comments.body: Everybody needs to lighten up. The Rings of Power is a visually beautiful and well acted Tolkien-adjacent show. No, it isn’t fine art, but I certainly enjoy it.

comments.name: Hastings
comments.body:
I can't relate to Galadriel being a plucky elf in her 20s who is racing around, sword in hand, and being adventurous. By the end of the second age she has to be at around 5000 years old. She would be a wise, stable, and mature adult not some ridiculous Generation whatever. 

And, Gandalf came in the 3rd age (year 1000). It's in Unfinished Tales and other works, including the appendix in LOTR. A few minor references Tolkien made about Gandalf maybe arriving for a bit in the 2nd age aren't enough to develop a story line.

This series would have been better set in the first age and the elves trying to retrieve the silmarils.

comments.name: Biker
comments.body: I've never read the source material. I Loved the first two seasons as they seemed to do a good job of drawing out the characters, their conflicts and the mysteries driving them. I'm enjoying the 3rd but it lacks the tension. Closest was whether the orc general was to be trusted...

comments.name: Gabriel
comments.body:
I read LOTR a dozen times at least, the Hobbit too, and the Silmarillion thrice or so. The latter was never as good a read, it’s more biblical and less of a character-focused narrative. But it’s good history for those of us who like the world Tolkien created. 

That being said, the three movies of The Hobbit were a slog that should’ve been reduced to about two hours in total. The Rings of Power, on other hand, is a decent and often fun depiction of the second age. Yes, some of the dialog is pretty horrid, but overall it’s visually stunning and a pleasant diversion for those of us who like to immerse ourselves in Middle Earth during our free time. (Particularly since it seems we might never get any more books in the Game of Thrones series. Yes, I’m throwing shade at you, George Martin.)

By comparison, is TROP as good as the first Star Wars trilogy (episodes 4 through 6)? No. But it’s probably ant least as good ans episodes 1 through 3. And much better than some of the SW spinoffs. 

I’m in for a penny, in for a pound.

comments.name: Eugene
comments.body: I often use critics as my bellwether to decide what to take a chance on. And I usually agree with them. But in this case, I disagree. I think the Rings of Power is great, and I’m a huge LOTR fan. I even took courses about it in college. I think both a new and classic vision can live side by side.

comments.name: Jxb
comments.body: I don’t not like RoP, but the first two seasons were static and saturated in a way that reliably lulled me into a stately sleep. And I mean that as a compliment—in this agitating time, having a show that helps you wind down is a beautiful thing. Most of the complaints here relate to the fact that this is true long form storytelling, which is rare on TV these days. Nowadays we just want to get to the fireworks factory. And the first two seasons did deliver a few of those moments, like the creation of Mordor and Mount Doom, just not enough for most. The third season seems to have heard this criticism and has sped up the storytelling in the manner of the later seasons of GoT. I’m enjoying it so far and hope it stays on the rails, unlike GoT. Again, I don’t dislike this show and want to see it succeed.

comments.name: Ovid
comments.body:
I stopped in the middle of episode 2 of season 1. From the first five minutes one can tell something is very wrong with it. Drawn out to a glacial pace, the dialogue is meaningless and has no point, as in the example James cited. And the identity politics were distracting to say the least. There was a 20 minute scene of a dwarf and his plus sized black dwarf wife just talking over dinner that was baffling, and it dawns on one that the show creators have no idea where they're going with all this. 

I read that each season costs Bezos about $500 million, but to cancel the series would only cost him $20 million termination fee. I wonder why he keeps spending $500 million on another season. Wheel of Time seasons 2 and 3 were incredible: they should have kept that show going and canceled this Rings of Power.

comments.name: Uncommon Sense
comments.body:
Sigh. So many tries at adapting JRR Tolkien’s legendarium to the screen. And so many fails. And part of that may be that much of his prequel work was more scholarly world creating than telling engaging stories. 

Peter Jackson’s LOTR pulled it off, with three great films. Yet even those, like many screen adaptations of complex literary works, fell short in being true to the trilogy.  

And since the execrable Hobbit series of films, 
I’ve just given up on watching any of the recent  Tolkien adaptions. They’re an assault on my memory. 

To digress, now let’s see what the film version of The Magician’s Nephew will be like. IMO it is right after The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe as the best in CS Lewis’ Narnia canon. I greatly fear how it may be butchered.

articles.title: In ‘The Rings of Power,’ I.P.-Based TV Loses Its Magic
articles.summary: The costly Tolkien extravaganza, now in its third season, is a monument to the scale and forgettability of many of TV’s franchise spinoffs.

comments.name: Curious
comments.body: Data should belong to the person it is about or to the person that created it.  This should not be a sellable commodity.

comments.name: The Wheel

Something smells here, and this deserves a Congressional investigation.  The new Congress has so much work to do, it will take at least two years to start to undo all the damage Trump has caused.

comments.name: ElSol

comments.name: Catfriend
comments.body: Remember when Google motto was "Don't Be Evil"? Yeah, that didn't age well.

comments.name: Jeff
comments.body: To those who say none of Stern’s buildings would make the list: I’d argue that some of his firm’s greatest achievements are urban buildings around the world that few people notice, precisely because they’re so thoughtfully woven into their surroundings, while many of his peers reached for some contrarian gesture to stand out. Much of his commercial work, like the shingle-style houses that defined his early practice, has aged gracefully. The same can’t be said of the current iteration of 2 Columbus Circle, the Edward Durell Stone building he fought to save. He left a tremendous legacy of design and scholarship.

comments.name: Gerry
comments.body: None of Stern’s buildings will ever appear on such a list.

comments.name: madamekou
comments.body: This list shows a fine eye applied with historical knowledge--unlike the National Civic Society, which thinks every public building should be in the classical style and unlike the president who has a crude notion of how architecture expresses power. Stern did the classical drag for wealthy clients, but could see a larger range of aesthetic value.

comments.name: Alan R
comments.body: There is little built in NYC that can resist being torn down by  real estate interests. Surprising a few marvels of outstanding architecture are still standing. Typical of American success. An example of the lack of values. If you go to Europe, you can see in major cities, the preservation of certain buildings that have lasting value. Here not so much.

comments.name: Ceadan
comments.body: I can appreciate that, historically, these buildings are representative of the twentieth century's mindless brutality and inhumanity and celebrations of its coarse and tasteless greed.  On the other hand "modern architecture" is little more than a synonym for "eyesore."  How many of these do we really need?

comments.name: Ruben Fernandez
comments.body: Sorry to ean Donnelly Library was demolished. Replacement doesn’t even come close in value or aesthetic.

comments.name: Metaphor
comments.body:
I remember watching a retrospective on the Rolling Stones with footage of fans in the mid-1960s. One young female fan said about the Stones, "They're so ugly they're good looking." Her point, I think, was that The Beatles were clean-cut and cute, but the Stones had an air of grungy nastiness that translated into flair and style.

That's kind of how I feel about the original version of 2 Columbus Circle. It's so ugly it's good looking. The building's sheer presence exuded panache hiding behind its austere facade.

comments.name: JGO
comments.body: I love the International industrial style. What is bad about NYC now, besides the bicycles, is the new buildings in Hudson Yards.

articles.title: 30 Years Ago, Robert A.M. Stern Asked New York to Preserve These Modern Buildings
articles.summary: Two from the architect’s 1996 list of 35 have been demolished. Here’s what happened to the rest of the structures Stern sought to protect.

comments.name: Eleanor
comments.body: A key claim in this piece is: "President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia is NOT ready to engage in serious negotiations on a peace settlement for Ukraine, according to Western intelligence assessments, even as he prepares to meet with President Trump on Thursday in China." Who are these Western Intelligence Assessors? Are these western assessors same NATO members, or even Zelensky, who provoked the war with Russia or those who favor continued war with Russia? Are they the same people who continue to vilify Russia? Thankfully, Trump, in a rare moment of his presidency, is open to diplomatic relations with Russia. Maybe these assessors, who have conveniently forgotten about NATO's sabotaging the war preventing and war ending Minsk and Istanbul talks, are more concerned about opposing Trump's peace overtures than in negotiating a peaceful settlement. Please,  tell us who these western tell as

comments.body: Russia (“Putin”) will continue the war in Ukraine because it is doing well on the battlefield and sees a good chance of realizing its main objectives: preventing a hostile NATO presence on its borders and reconfiguring the landscape of security in Europe. "In rigorous studies of thousands of chief executives, police officers and financial advisers, those who used the Ashley Madison website for sexual infidelity had significantly higher rates of professional misconduct than those who did not." 

I'm familiar with the study. It uses the Ashley Madison data leak to compare likelihoods of having an account on the cheating site for professions who did and did not commit professional misconduct. The base rates are low (2.9% vs. ~1.3%), so yes people who commit misconduct in one domain are more likely to commit in another but most people who were on the cheating website never did. So it's misleading to assume that b/c someone cheated they are a big misconduct risk. 

Now, this case may be different given its particulars (e.g., these were work contacts and employees), and I'm not defending Huang or Nvidia, but Grant is being a bit too loose with the empirics in his argument. Plenty of people who cheat should not be disqualified from their professional position b/c of it.

comments.name: Mayor Jared Kraham
comments.body:
I spoke to the New York Times at length about this — the inherent challenges of maintaining century-old carousels, and Binghamton's commitment to preserving them for future generations. Unfortunately, my perspective on the carousels was not included. 
 
The issue of keeping our community’s carousels running is not a matter of local government prioritizing funding and maintenance — we are more than willing to spend what’s needed. The challenge lies in the scarcity of companies still in operation nationwide that deal with antique mechanical ride systems and artisan historic restoration. 

A carousel is equal parts art and amusement ride. In Binghamton’s case, add “historic artifact” to the mix. Every horse must be hand-painted within historic guidelines. Every mechanical part must be custom fabricated. The scarcity of this craftsmanship means unpredictable timelines and frequent delays. 

When a breakdown inevitably happens, our dedicated Parks Department employees work wonders, but they are not antique carousel technicians. Larger issues mean the City has to rely on a few outside vendors to travel in from hours away. With other carousel operators nationwide needing the same services, the wait time is rarely quick. 

Broome County’s carousels are monuments of civic pride that bring a warmth and nostalgia to residents who remember riding them as kids, and a responsibility to preserve that tradition for future generations.

Housing prices are good, with large, older houses that are comfy and spacious. Lots of parks, abundant beauty in the area, a thriving downtown, many cultural institutions, and the "Strip" is a great market area. The North Side used to be a pass through to the mills, but with the mills gone, has taken on a life of its own. Heading out the other direction is Lawrenceville, which has become a haven for younger people. Then there is the University area, with the Univ of Pittsburgh, Carnegie Mellon and Carlow College, as well as the Carnegie Library, Museum, concert hall, hospitals, Phipps Conservatory, Schenley Park and more. It's a great town, sometimes called, "little New York," because of the concentration of so much into a doable town with wonderful neighborhoods.
